name: Erik Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for taking part, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and your answers are confidential. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead operator on the press line at Tallis Panels. We make chipboard, the stuff inside cheap furniture and kitchen worktops. Wood chips and glue go in one end, and a sixty-metre press squeezes them into boards at about two hundred degrees. I watch the screens, walk the line, check board thickness and sort out the forming station when the chips clump.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Finding patterns. I started logging every stoppage in a spreadsheet two years ago, and I use an AI chat every day to help me spot what they have in common. Turns out half our jams happen when the chips come from one supplier on wet days. I showed the manager and she changed the order schedule. That felt good, even if the pay didn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Bit of an anticlimax, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and people got carried away. At work I'd say keep using it for the boring stuff, like I do with the stoppage log. Online I'd stay out of it; the arguments are tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the problem stays the same: I'm good at this and I'm paid like I'm not. I've got about two weeks of money saved, Maya (my girlfriend) rents a chair at a hair salon and her money goes up and down, and Tallis is the only board plant for eighty kilometres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep improving the line and keep the stoppage log, because that's how I get noticed. I'd ask for a pay review in January with my numbers on paper. And I'd grow the side thing I do, fixing 3D printers for people and selling spare parts online, which makes about a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit frustrated. Like I'm running fast on a short lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on paper for the pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stoppage hours down from forty a month to twenty-six since I started the log. I'd ask the AI to help me turn that into money saved, because managers listen to money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the review says no, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the printer repairs get more of my evenings. I wouldn't leave Tallis yet, there's nothing else around. But I'd be building a way out.

Maya's **salon income** swings, and Tallis is the only board plant nearby.

Grow his **3D printer repair** side business.
Keep the **stoppage log** running with AI.
feel: **Frustrated**, like running fast on a **short lead**.

steps.text: Request a January pay review with stoppage data
Take on more 3D printer repairs in the evenings
Keep logging stoppages and analysing them with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I could work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a threat, if you learn the tools. At work I'd offer to show people how I use the AI with the stoppage log. I'd probably post a short video about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The office planning and buying change first, and my job is half hands-on and half watching data. I'm already the guy who speaks both languages. My worry is that Tallis won't pay more for that, just expect it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Tallis to let me trial sensors on the press, the cheap vibration ones, and feed the data into an AI tool. I'd do an online course in industrial data, evenings. And I'd keep the printer business going as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Excited, a bit greedy for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tallis would expect it but not pay. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After a year, if there's no raise, I'd take my results to the board plants up north. Maya would hate moving, but a CV that says I cut stoppages by a third gets calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul on the night shift. He's good with his hands but he hates screens. I'd sit with him, but some people just won't.

fieldNote: He sees himself as a clear **winner** in this scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a sprint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a plan from government, quickly, because most of my mates aren't me. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it. Not marching, but I'd write to whoever represents us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 an AI can read the stoppage data better than me, so my clever bit is gone. I've got three years on the hands-on part, until the robots can clear a clumped forming station. I'm adaptable, but I've got two weeks of savings, and you can't adapt on nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year becoming the person who installs and looks after the robots when they arrive. I'd push the printer business hard, because people will want things fixed, and I'd try to get it to five hundred a month. And Maya and I would cut back hard: no holiday, cheaper phone plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but my brain would be running all night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look after the robots. Would those jobs exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, for a while. Fewer than the jobs they replace, and the robots will get better at fixing each other. I'd be buying time, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Maya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say her job might actually outlast mine, because nobody wants a robot cutting their hair yet. Then I'd say we need to save like it's winter.

steps.text: Volunteer to install and maintain Tallis's first robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to train up, and if you're young, this is a good moment to jump. I'd tell the younger lads at Tallis to learn robotics, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is close to perfect for me. I'd have time to get a proper automation qualification and save a bit. By 2031 the thinking AI arrives, and I'd want to already be the person who knows how to run AI on a factory floor. Then I'd have three more years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an automation technician course next year, part-time, and ask Tallis to help pay. I'd put the printer money into a savings account, not the bike fund. And I'd look at a better-paid plant within a couple of hours, once I had the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more fired up than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said save the printer money. How much a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About twelve hundred, if I'm strict. Twelve hundred saved would be three months of rent, the biggest cushion I've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tallis could close before the robots even come, if the owners decide it's cheaper to build a new robot plant somewhere else. That's the real fear. Then all my clever plans need a new address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable for someone my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for not getting ready. I'd say a decade is time to retrain twice. At work I'd keep showing people the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is fine for me, maybe good. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come, with ten years of learning behind me. I might even run my own repair business by then. The money now is the only thing that bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the printer side into a proper small business over three years, maybe with a little workshop. I'd do the automation course at my own pace. And I'd stay at Tallis while it all builds, because the steady wage pays the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite optimistic, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your own business. Would that survive the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not as repairs. But by then I'd know what people actually need, and maybe that's setting up robots in small shops. Ten years is long enough to change direction twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maya and I would probably talk about a place of our own sooner. Not buying, we can't, but a bigger flat with a garage for the workshop.

A decade is enough time to **retrain twice**, and he'd keep showing colleagues the tools.

Stay at **Tallis** for the steady wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm quick, but quick doesn't help when you've got two weeks of savings and three years of runway. What would help is cheap or free short courses in robot maintenance, and some kind of help with rent while you switch. Not a handout forever, just a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether the people who own the plants would share any of the savings. The plant saved a lot from my stoppage log and I got a thank-you email. With robots that gap gets bigger.

headlineQuote: The plant saved a lot from my stoppage log and I got a thank-you email.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old** lead operator on a chipboard press line at Tallis Panels.
He uses **AI daily** to analyse stoppages and runs a small 3D printer repair side business.
Lower-paid with about **two weeks saved**, he lives with Maya, a hairdresser with uneven income.
Pragmatic and **adaptable**, he sees steady change as a chance and plans automation training.
Only the **two-year** warning worries him: adaptability, he says, needs money behind it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: two weeks of savings and only three years of runway.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap or free **robot maintenance** courses and **rent help** as a bridge.
